articles.headline: Victor Wembanyama gives his honest take on having a signature move in the NBA
keyFacts: San Antonio Spurs player Victor Wembanyama stated he does not currently have a single signature offensive move like other NBA stars.
Wembanyama explained in an interview that his goal is to develop go-to moves rather than explicitly trying to create a signature shot.
Wembanyama noted that balancing individual skill development with team success is a constant challenge for players.
body: San Antonio Spurs superstar Victor Wembanyama has cemented his place as one of the best players in the NBA. He is a defensive monster who can protect the rim like no other. On the other hand, he can be dominant on offense, but he does not have that signature move that other top players do.

In the current crop of players, there are stars with go-to moves like Shai Gilgeous-Alexander's step-back and Nikola Jokic's Sombor Shuffle. Wembanyama does not have that, and it seems that he does not plan on having only one go-to move.
Victor Wembanyama speaks on having signature moves on offense

Considering that Wembanyama is a 7'5" behemoth, there are plenty of ways he can have a signature move. Megastars like Shaquille O'Neal used their physical strengths to their advantage with his drop step and Kareem Abdul-Jabbar with his sky hook.

The latter is what people want to see from Wembanyama, which is an unblockable shot, especially with his height and length. However, that is harder than most people realize because no one has replicated the sky hook's effectiveness ever since Kareem retired in the late 1980s.

Wembanyama has admitted that he is working on his game behind the scenes. That is a good sign for the Spurs because they will have Wembanyama as a more versatile player on offense, which only boosts their chances of winning.

"Of course. Hopefully, yeah. It's always a challenge to balance individual development and team goals because for every one of us, we're not out there to work on our game. We're here to win games... I feel like a signature shot is something you look back on and make the conclusion this is their signature shot. So it's not the goal to create a signature shot, but go-to moves; yes it is," Wembanyama said in a post-game interview.

That is a healthy mindset to have, as there is a delicate balance between individual development and team success. Sometimes, a player has to hone their skills to fit their goals, and Wembanyama seems to be looking for the right balance at the moment.

articles.headline: Tyrese Maxey admits he is tired of the 76ers having to come back from big deficits
keyFacts: The Philadelphia 76ers achieved a 6-1 record for the 2026-27 NBA season following a 109-104 victory over the Charlotte Hornets.
Philadelphia player Tyrese Maxey stated after the game that he is tired of the team repeatedly overcoming double-digit deficits.
Maxey indicated that the team aims to establish early leads so they can win comfortably and rest star players.
body: The Philadelphia 76ers are off to a superb start to the 2026-27 NBA season, with a 6-1 record. This comes after their latest win against the Charlotte Hornets, 109-104. It was not an easy victory because they had to come back from a double-digit deficit yet again.

That was the fourth time they had to claw back from a double-digit deficit, so it seems that the 76ers are well aware of that problem. They do not want that to become an issue, so they are ready to put that behind them.
Tyrese Maxey does not want the 76ers to get complacent after another comeback

The 76ers have been one of the most impressive teams this season, as they are actually living up to the hype. The same cannot be said for some teams this season, but the 76ers do know they are not a perfect team.

They have started with six wins and a single loss, but there could be some problems with how they approach games. The 76ers have the tendency to let the opponent take a big lead, then they rely on a big run to come back and win the game.

While that leads to some satisfying wins, it is not the most sustainable approach to games. The 76ers need to establish themselves from the jump, so they can win comfortably. It seems that star player Tyrese Maxey has the same sentiment.

"I don't want to do that; I'm tired of that. This group some fighters, man. We went up, went down, came back, you know, we're very competitive. The game's not over 'til it's over, and that's what I really like about this group," Maxey said in his post-game interview after the win against the Hornets.

With all of the awesome players the 76ers have on the roster, they are ready to win and be healthy. If they can have more comfortable results, they can afford to rest some of their star players. Maxey would love that, as they are building better contuinity for their goals of winning a title.

articles.headline: 9 Years Later, Jon Bernthal’s Action Series Is a Masterpiece From Start to Finish
keyFacts: Jon Bernthal played Frank Castle in the action television series The Punisher, which originally debuted nine years ago.
Polygon reported that the series features the character relying on military training and weapons rather than superpowers to seek justice.
Polygon stated that Bernthal returned to the role following the series' 2019 end as Disney+ brought back Marvel's Netflix heroes.
body: Ever since superhero movies and television became popular, fans have debated which actors are the perfect fit for their characters. The debate has escalated over the years, especially when multiple actors have played iconic characters like Superman and Spider-Man. Nine years ago, one of the best actor-to-character pairings came when Jon Bernthal took on Frank Castle in The Punisher. In the process, Bernthal delivered one of the grittiest and most action-packed comic book adaptations in history.

Bernthal first played Castle in Daredevil, where he laid the groundwork for his eventual solo debut. There, he embarked on a hunt for the men who killed his wife and children, coming to physical and moral blows with Matt Murdock along the way. The Punisher continues this character journey, but throws a few wrinkles into Frank's way: a partner in tech expert David Liberman, aka "Micro" (Ebon Moss-Bachrach), the return of fellow soldier Billy Russo (Ben Barnes), and Dinah Madani (Amber Rose Revah), a Homeland Security agent determined to bring him in.
'The Punisher' doesn't shy away from the character's complexity

Part of the appeal of the Punisher is that, unlike other Marvel characters, he has no special abilities; he relies mostly on his military training and arsenal of firearms to deliver his own brand of justice to the wicked. Yet he also realizes that no matter how many criminals he kills, it won't fill the void within him. In the afterword to Punisher: The King of Killers, Jason Aaron argues that Frank Castle's life is a tragedy. The Punisher series deals with this, showing that Castle suffers immense PTSD from his time as a soldier in addition to the loss of his family, and that he only truly feels at peace when he slaughters the wicked. Bernthal expanded upon this in an interview, saying that it's what drove him to play the character:
"He ain't got a f***ing cape. He ain't got any superpowers. He's a f***ing tortured, angry father and husband who's living in this unbelievable world of darkness and loss and torment."

Both seasons of The Punisher also give Castle plenty of chances to vent his fury upon the guilty. In Season 1, it's revealed that Russo is behind the events that led to Castle's family's deaths, and Castle eventually takes his revenge by grinding his former friend's face into a mirror. This doesn't kill Russo, but transforms him into the heavily scarred villain Jigsaw. That scene also one of many blood-soaked action sequences in The Punisher's run; whether it's through firefights, knives, or his bare hands, Castle finds many ways to deliver death.
Jon Bernthal recently returned to play the Punisher

When The Punisher ended in 2019, it felt like the end of Jon Bernthal's tenure as the character. That proved short-lived, thanks to Disney+ resurrecting Marvel's Netflix heroes with Daredevil: Born Again.

Bernthal wasn't done with the character yet and co-starred in Spider-Man: Brand New Day. If fans want to see more of his work, they should definitely revisit The Punisher as it's brutal, uncompromising, and hard-hitting — just like Frank Castle.

articles.headline: ‘Like Kashmir’: How a toxic marble dump yard became a tourist spot in India
keyFacts: A 300-acre marble slurry dump yard in Kishangarh has become a popular tourist attraction resembling a snowy landscape.
Toxic dust from the site contaminates water and causes respiratory illness, a university study and local residents report.
The National Green Tribunal directed the state pollution control board to monitor the site and penalize violating marble units.
body: Kishangarh, India – As Bagharam Gurjar kneels to pull weeds from his maize field in western India’s Rajasthan state, the sound of his wife coughing nearby makes him restless.
“Everything gets ruined when dust settles on the soil,” says Gurjar, 53, barely looking up.
“May God make everything right,” replies his wife between bouts of chronic cough. “Otherwise, it becomes difficult to grow crops.”
The Gurjars are among nearly 5,000 people living in the vicinity of what has turned out to be one of the most unusual tourist destinations in India.

Their village, Bhogiyawas, is just 6km (4 miles) from Kishangarh, where a 300-acre (121-hectare) marble slurry dumping yard resembles a snow-clad landscape, attracting hundreds of tourists every day in an otherwise arid state.

Locally known as a “Snow Yard”, the landfill in Rajasthan’s Ajmer district is the largest of its kind in Asia. Its pristine white hills and slopes with water-filled pits provide a surreal backdrop for visitors, who get free entry to the site.

Newlyweds pose against the snowy backdrop or the blue artificial lake, while couples soon to get married organise pre-wedding photoshoots. Social media influencers throng the landfill to make reels. Music videos and movies are also frequently shot here.

“Everyone, right from my five-year-old niece to my mother, loves it very much. Their first impression was that this looks like Kashmir,” Salim Shahzada, a businessman from Uttar Pradesh state, told Al Jazeera, referring to Indian-administered Kashmir.
Shahzada said he had visited the place a couple of times and decided to bring his family along this time. But he had no idea about the health and environmental problems linked to the dumping yard.
“I do not have much knowledge about this place or its ill effects. I only know that this is where marble cutting waste is dumped and that the hill itself is made of this waste,” he said.

Kishangarh, a marble and granite hub, is home to nearly 1,200 processing units, with the total daily business estimated at more than 160 million rupees ($1.7m), providing jobs to about 25,000 people, according to the Federation of Indian Granite and Stone Industry.

Every day, nearly 1,000 tankers carry slurry from those units and empty roughly 5,500 tonnes of waste on the government-allotted dump site, which, for the people living nearby, has turned into a health hazard.
Gurjar said the yard has affected residents in at least six villages. “How many problems can I even tell you about? If there were just one or two, we could deal with them,” he said.

“But here, almost everything is going wrong because of the dumping yard. People like me are suffering from chest infections, dental problems and skin allergies. It does not matter whether they are children or elderly people; everyone is suffering.”
Gurjar said he and his wife are forced to take regular medicines for chest infections or skin problems.

Aditi Goyal, a general physician at Ajmer’s Ganga Narayan Hospital, said the residents of Kishangarh face several health risks, mainly respiratory and skin problems. She said the workers in the marble processing units are more vulnerable to chronic illnesses because of prolonged exposure to toxic dust.
“Over the last couple of years, cases of respiratory problems have increased significantly in this area because people are exposed to dust from the dumping yard,” Goyal told Al Jazeera.

“However, dust from industrial waste is not the only issue. People in Kishangarh, who are mostly farmers, also suffer from infections caused by dust coming from the soil,” she said, advising people to wear masks to protect themselves from dust.
The same dust settles on the fields, hardening the soil and making it difficult to grow crops.

A study led by Laxmi Kant Sharma, professor in the department of environmental science at the Central University of Rajasthan, found that the concentration of lead silicate in Kishangarh’s soil was several times higher than normal, indicating extreme contamination.
“Since the waste particles are smaller than 75 micrometres, they can spread far and wide, making the soil infertile,” the study said.

The study also found that the concentration of PM2.5 exceeds the limit of ambient air quality standards. “Several people may be suffering from silicosis. The government needs to take immediate action to prevent the situation from getting out of hand,” it said.

Ugam Singh, another resident of Bhogiyawas, remembers when things were different. The continuous dumping of slurry slowly changed the landscape and the lives of people in Kishangarh, says the 65-year-old.
“Nowadays, the situation has worsened to such an extent that even the groundwater is no longer fit for consumption,” Singh said.

“The fluoride levels in the water are so high that it tastes salty. My teeth have started decaying and my bones have become weak,” he added, pointing to his teeth, which appeared pale, pitted and worn.

Singh said the residents of villages surrounding the dump yard have complained to the authorities, including officials of the Rajasthan State Pollution Control Board (RSPCB). But their requests fell on deaf ears.

“What I have come to understand is that it does not matter which government is in power. No one listens to the poor. To make the rich richer, the government sacrifices the interests of people like us. It feels as though our lives have no value,” Singh said.
“Even today all we want is for this marble slurry dumping to stop so that we can breathe freely again and our fields can become green and productive once again.”
Singh also claims that if residents of all the villages around the dumping yard were properly examined, almost every household would have someone suffering from respiratory problems such as asthma.

Last year, local environmentalist Drupad Malik filed a case before the National Green Tribunal over the harmful health and environmental effects of the Kishangarh dumping yard. The tribunal observed that unregulated dumping of marble slurry was contaminating groundwater and air. It directed the RSPCB to enforce monitoring, conduct sample inspections and penalise the marble processing units violating environmental norms.
Al Jazeera reached out to a senior official at the RSPCB’s regional office in Kishangarh, but she refused to speak on the matter.

Central University’s Sharma said the areas surrounding the Kishangarh dumping yard are unfit for human settlement. He said his research was shared with state authorities, but nothing was done to improve the environmental conditions in the area.

“There is a dire need to shift the dumping yard to another place where there is no human contact. This area has become extremely toxic and vulnerable to severe diseases. I am surprised that people are allowed to visit the site without masks and even have food there,” Sharma told Al Jazeera.
“I have forwarded several suggestions, including installing tile units, as [marble] slurry is used in tile manufacturing. This could, to some extent, help reduce pollution in Kishangarh,” he added.
Meanwhile, Ram Lal, a resident of Tokra village, about a 15-minute drive from Bhogiyawas, appealed to the government to find an alternative site for dumping the marble slurry.
“Kishangarh is full of slurry, and it is time to shift the dumping yard out of here to some other place where no one will suffer for at least two to three decades,” Lal told Al Jazeera.
“We also demand that free medical camps be set up to assess people whose health has declined because of the fine dust particles that have been flying in the air and settling here for years,” he said.
“No one from our village can afford it if someone develops a disease that costs thousands of rupees to treat.”

articles.headline: Are the US midterms going to see a blue wave of Democrats winning seats – or a blue flood?
keyFacts: Democrats lead Republicans by 11 points on the generic congressional ballot ahead of next week's midterm elections, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll.
Analysts said that rising living costs, tariffs, and the Iran war have damaged President Donald Trump's standing with voters.
Voters will decide control of Congress, 36 state governorships, and thousands of legislative seats next week.
body: He spoke admiringly of a senator’s posterior. He baselessly accused a Muslim candidate of being a terrorist. He boasted about his renovations of the White House. He quipped that his own supporters couldn’t afford a hamburger at his Mar-a-Lago club. Every now and then, he spoke about the cost of living, and other everyday concerns of voters.

Donald Trump has held dozens of campaign rallies before next week’s US midterm elections. The 80-year-old remains convinced that he can prove the doubters wrong again and help Republicans retain control of the US Congress. But it was five words he uttered at this summer’s Republican convention in Dallas that could seal his party’s fate: “Pretend I’m on the ticket.”

That plea was music to the ears of Democrats. It helped ensure that the midterms will deliver a national verdict on Trump’s second term in the White House. And opinion polls suggest that the judgment will be damning, piercing his aura of invincibility, reshaping the final two years of his presidency and setting the stage for a fierce battle to succeed him.

“Donald Trump nationalised these races, and now they’ll lose seats because of it,” said Michael Steele, a former chair of the Republican National Committee. “He made himself the referendum. Individual candidates wanted to run their individual races but he told them: ‘Put me on the ballot.’ He has political instincts for himself, but no political instincts for the party.”

Pain is the norm for White House incumbents when the midterms roll around. In 1994, Bill Clinton suffered a 54-seat setback in the House of Representatives; in 2010, Barack Obama lost 63; in 2018, Trump himself lost 40. He seems unlikely to defy history this time. Trump goes into the elections with the lowest approval rating of any president before the midterms since Harry Truman’s Democrats were crushed 80 years ago.

The coalition that in 2024 powered Trump to the greatest comeback in modern political history has suffered blow after blow: his failure to fully release the Jeffrey Epstein files detailing ties of the elite to the child sex offender; the growth of datacentres in rural communities; an eight-month-old war in Iran that he promised would be over in weeks; a relentless rise in the cost of fuel and food.

The anger over Trump’s broken promises has been compounded by a whiff of corruption, and the perception that he is using the presidency to enrich himself and his family. He accepted a plane from Qatar to use as Air Force One, decorated the Oval Office in gold, demolished the White House East Wing to make way for a $400m ballroom and is planning a triumphal arch in Washington. His personal fortune meanwhile has surged – from $2.3bn in 2024 to $6.5bn, according to Forbes.
‘Much more macro than Maga’

With Republicans clinging to a paper-thin 218–214 margin in the House and 53–47 lead in the Senate, opinion polls indicate a rising “blue wave”. A recent Reuters/Ipsos survey gave Democrats an 11-point lead, 47% to 36%, on the generic congressional ballot, while Trump’s approval rating stood at 32%. Voters will also choose governors in 36 states and three US territories, and decide thousands of state legislative contests.

Tens of millions of early votes have already been cast, with habitual Republican turnout lagging behind Democratic participation in critical battlegrounds. So dire is the environment for Republicans that conservative Super Pacs backed by billionaire Elon Musk, who has poured $366m into saving Republican candidates, are being forced to dump emergency funds into strongholds like Kansas, Iowa and Texas.

Trump won the presidency in 2024 after promising to curb inflation and lower prices; instead, the opposite has happened. Across the country, voters are confronting an affordability crisis exacerbated by two defining choices of Trump’s second term: a sweeping regime of foreign tariffs and the fateful decision to launch airstrikes on Iran in February.

Chris Matthews, a political commentator and former presidential speechwriter and congressional aide, said: “He’s losing on cost of living and affordability. Older people on limited incomes are focusing on what it costs to live each month. It’s much more macro than Maga. No matter what he does for Maga people, the power of macroeconomics is much stronger and people are going to vote against him.”

The economic fallout of the Iran war, which Trump frequently downplays as a “little detour”, has reverberated across global energy markets. Diesel prices have soared, sending shock waves through agriculture and freight transport from the Central valley of California to the grain belts of Iowa and Ohio.

Elaine Kamarck, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and former official in the Clinton White House, points out that voters can directly attribute their economic misery to the president. “There’s a very clear line between his actions and the things people don’t like,” she said.

“It’s going to be the tariffs and it’s going to be the war: both self-inflicted wounds. He didn’t have to raise tariffs; that was his theory of the world, which turned out to be wrong. Bombing nuclear sites in Iran was one thing, but going to all-out war turned out to be a mistake. Voters connect his actions to things they don’t like.”

This frustration is fuelling an energetic mobilisation among Democratic candidates, particularly women running in districts that once seemed out of reach. Jessica Mackler, the president of Emilys List, which is backing 247 female candidates this cycle, notes that voters feel the economic system is actively stacked against them.

“Voters understand that the corruption coming out of Washington is directly linked to why they can’t get ahead, and why they find it so hard to make ends meet,” Mackler said. “Cost of living is a huge driver but voters are desperate for new leadership who have lived their pain and understand it.”
A ‘devastating referendum’ on Trump

For months, Republican strategists urged their candidates in tight suburban races to keep national politics at arm’s length, and focus on local accomplishments, perhaps hoping that Trump might quietly concentrate on his day job in Washington. Instead, the president has embarked on a whirlwind tour across the country, denouncing Democrats as “communists” while touting a strong economy, secure border and historic drop in violent crime.

But Steele, a co-host of the MS Now network’s the Weeknight, argues that core conservative voters feel increasingly betrayed by a president who promised to avoid foreign entanglements and bring down costs. “Donald Trump lied to his tribe … He said he wouldn’t engage us in foreign wars; we’re now turning the corner into a year of a war he started and people are saying: ‘I can’t even afford to put gas in my car.’”

Perhaps no development in the 2026 midterms is more alarming to Republican strategists than the dramatic erosion of support among Latino voters. In 2024, Trump made historic inroads with Latino men, sparking triumphant declarations of a permanent multiethnic, working-class coalition.

Yet no sooner had he taken the oath of office than he unleashed an aggressive, high-visibility deportation campaign featuring heavily armed Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids in cities and agricultural hubs.

Larry Jacobs, founder and director of the Center for the Study of Politics and Governance at the University of Minnesota, said: “Donald Trump launched his radical deportation strategy and it has powerfully alienated the fastest-growing part of the electorate.

“A year ago, Republicans thought they had established a new Hispanic coalition that would guarantee five new seats in Texas alone. They may lose all of them. Economics is a driving factor, but opposition to Trump’s deportation policies has contributed massively to the magnitude of the defections.”

Henry Olsen, a senior fellow at the Ethics and Public Policy Center thinktank in Washington, notes that the Latino shift is visible across public polling and state-level data, saying: “Whether it’s a 15-point shift or a 30-point shift, it’s a big deal. Unless every piece of evidence we have is wrong, Latino voters are having serious buyers’ remorse.”

This dynamic is evident in Texas, where no Democrat has won statewide office since 1994. James Talarico, a 37-year-old state representative and former public school teacher who preaches a gospel of social justice, is taking on Republican state attorney general Ken Paxton in the most expensive Senate race in history.

Paxton, a staunch Trump ally, has been bogged down by years of corruption allegations, personal scandal and securities fraud charges. Despite $300m in outside Republican spending, led by Musk, Talarico has a narrow lead in most polls.

Jacobs views Texas as a bellwether for the post-Trump Republican party. “If Paxton loses, it’s going to send a very powerful signal to future Republican leaders about how they handle immigration,” he said. “It proves that attacking the fastest-growing part of the electorate is political suicide. Texas is a devastating referendum on Donald Trump.”
A test for Democrats

While Democrats appear heavily favoured to pick up the four net seats required to capture the House of Representatives, their path to taking the Senate is a steeper climb. Yet because of Trump’s dismal approval ratings and the economic shock of the Iran war, the Senate battlefield has expanded into states that voted for Trump by double digits in 2024.

In Ohio, former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown is mounting a comeback bid against incumbent Republican Jon Husted. Brown, a grizzled populist with deep ties to organised labour, has capitalised on working-class anger over fuel prices and plant closures, as well as local opposition to datacentres. In a peculiar recurring feature of his rallies in the state, Trump has frequently veered off-script to praise Husted’s physique. (“His ass was like a big piece of muscle,” according to the president.)

In Michigan, Republican Mike Rogers is up against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a 41-year-old doctor and former Detroit health director bidding to become the first Muslim senator in the US. Republicans have aggressively targeted El-Sayed over past foreign policy statements, while pro-Israel Super Pacs have poured millions of dollars into the state to defeat him. Trump has launched Islamophobic tirades, calling El-Sayed a “jihadist”.
Olsen said: “El-Sayed is the biggest test for progressives. If he wins stateside in an industrial heartland state like Michigan, progressives will argue they have the upper hand heading into 2028.”

However, Kamarck cautions against over-interpreting progressive strength. She insisted: “The progressives are a minuscule portion of the Democratic party. This is an overblown story. The moderates are winning the vast majority of these races across the country.”

In Maine, veteran Republican senator Susan Collins is fighting for her political life against Democrat Troy Jackson, a lumberjack and former president of the state senate. Collins has attempted to distance herself from Trump, appearing on the trail with independent former senator Joe Manchin, but Democrats have relentlessly hammered her votes for conservative supreme court justices and other Trump priorities.

In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola is mounting a challenge to Republican senator Dan Sullivan. The contest has become embroiled in a legal dispute after the justice department sought to block certification of a possible Peltola victory. Her allies reportedly helped recruit a decoy candidate with the name Dan Sullivan to confuse voters. Peltola’s campaign denies involvement.
‘He’ll do anything’

Election integrity remains a broader national concern. Trump’s repeated, unsubstantiated claims of election fraud have prompted Democrats and voting-rights organisations to prepare legal teams and observers for disputes or federal interference. The administration says federal election monitors will follow the law, and has denied plans to send troops or immigration agents to polling stations.

Tara Setmayer, a co-founder and chief executive of the Seneca Project, a women-led political action committee, said: “I am extremely worried. We have seen what Donald Trump has done when he had guardrails; now he has none. He has power and people who are aligned with him in the attack on our election integrity in positions of power.

“This is a great concern to me because Trump is looking at the sun setting on his presidency and we all know that he is deathly afraid of being out of power. He’ll do anything to stay in power, even if that means creating another constitutional crisis to try to stop Congress from being seated. We cannot suffer from a lack of imagination of what these people are capable of.”

A Democratic victory in either chamber will effectively stall Trump’s domestic legislative agenda, leaving his administration to rely on executive orders. Hakeem Jeffries, who would likely become the first Black speaker of the House, has pledged to immediately unleash subpoena power to investigate administration corruption, foreign policy decisions in Iran, and the personal financial enrichment of the Trump family.

Jacobs said: “It’s going to be a fistfight. I’m not expecting major legislation to pass. I think there will be extensive investigations of Donald Trump and his cabinet, and that’s what we’re going to get for two years.”

Steele believes that a Democratic House will immediately assert control over federal purse strings. “Congress will freeze money on projects like tearing down the East Wing for Trump’s ballroom, and they’ll reassert oversight over the Kennedy Center,” he said, referring to the national arts complex and living memorial to the 35th president. “Trump is effectively a lame duck now. The rest of the country knows his time is coming to an end.”

Indeed, before the last vote is counted, attention will likely turn to the presidential contest in 2028. For Republicans, a crushing midterm loss could accelerate the race to a post-Trump future. JD Vance is currently positioned as the heir apparent to the Maga movement, but figures such as the senator Ted Cruz of Texas and the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, could also be in contention.

Steele commented: “Republicans need to recognise that the future of the party does not rest solely with the Maga base. It rests with winning back the suburban, moderate and Hispanic voters this administration has isolated.”

Under pressure from a restive base, Democrats will also be preparing for a sprawling contest to decide the future direction of their party – and how it can turn the page on the Trump era. The next Democratic presidential candidate is equally uncertain, with outgoing California governor Gavin Newsom, Georgia senator Jon Ossoff, New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and even former vice-president and 2020 nominee Kamala Harris among those regularly mentioned.

Bill Whalen, a research fellow at the Hoover Institution thinktank in Stanford, California, said: “Voters are tired. When you combine high prices, the endless argument and the constant noise of Donald Trump, people want a change from the status quo.”
“On November 3, the voters are going to speak – and Donald Trump is not going to like what they have to say,” he predicted.

articles.headline: Lincoln Riley flips script on hot-seat chatter as USC's upset over Ohio State puts Trojans back in CFP picture
keyFacts: USC defeated second-ranked Ohio State 30-18, pushing the Trojans back into the College Football Playoff discussion.
Trojans quarterback Jayden Maiava threw for 222 yards and a touchdown, while running backs King Miller and Waymond Jordan added 126 rushing yards and two scores.
USC is now 7-2 overall and 4-2 in conference play, with remaining games against Indiana, Maryland, and UCLA.
body: Back against the wall and , Lincoln Riley delivered.
For only the , the Trojans toppled a ranked opponent under Riley, and it was a big one Saturday night against second-ranked Ohio State.

USC's 30-18 victory pushes Riley's squad back in the College Football Playoff discussion as part of the group that controls their own destiny entering the season's final month — with an outside shot at a Big Ten Championship Game appearance, too.

Poetically, this was his middle finger to and failure to meet expectations in Los Angeles. The Trojans still have elite opportunities remaining against Indiana — a one-loss team that's leaking oil with quarterback issues — and unbeaten UCLA during rivalry weekend.

Riley was 1-6 all-time against AP top-six opponents coming in, that lone victory coming in the form of a 31-16 decision over the Buckeyes in just his second game as a head coach back at Oklahoma in 2017.

"If I didn't want to be at this place, I wouldn't have come here in the first place," Riley said this week before the biggest win of his USC tenure. "I've had plenty of opportunities to leave. This is where I want to be. This is the right place for me. I'm the right person to be here. And that's as honest and transparent as I can be with you guys.

"I love it here. I mean, like I told you guys a lot of times, there's not many people in college football history that gave up what I gave up to come here. I don't care if it's 15 years down the line; that never should be taken lightly. It's certainly not taken lightly by me. I came here because I believe in this place and none of that has changed whatsoever."

USC put together a solid plan defensively to combat Heisman frontrunner Jeremiah Smith, limiting him to 83 yards receiving and a touchdown on 10 catches. Ohio State freshman quarterback Luke Fahey, who was making his first career start in place of injured Julian Sayin, never found a rhythm in the passing game and was chased out of the pocket throughout.
Trojans quarterback Jayden Maiava registered 222 yards through the air and a score, while running backs King Miller and Waymond Jordan combined for 126 yards and two touchdowns on the ground.
The loss for Ryan Day was only his sixth in 65 games against Big Ten competition with the Buckeyes.
USC's path to CFP berth, Big Ten Championship Game

Now 7-2 overall and 4-2 in conference play, the Trojans find themselves in a three-way tie for third in the conference standings after Week 9. With Indiana, Maryland and UCLA left, winning out gives USC three victories this season over ranked teams and puts the Trojans in prime position for an at-large CFP berth for the first time in program history.
To play in Indianapolis with a Big Ten title on the line, however, scenarios are a bit less clear:
- USC wins out and ...
- UCLA loses to Minnesota, Illinois or Michigan
- Northwestern loses to Iowa, Ohio State, Minnesota or Illinois
- Wisconsin loses to Rutgers, Maryland, Purdue or Minnesota
- Oregon loses to Ohio State, Michigan, Michigan State or Washington
- Ohio State loses to Northwestern, Nebraska or Michigan
- Nebraska loses to Washington, Illinois, Rutgers, Ohio State or Iowa
- Illinois loses to Nebraska, UCLA, Iowa or Northwestern (since it owns a common opponent win over Oregon)
- Iowa loses to Northwestern, Purdue, Illinois or Nebraska (since it owns a common opponent win over Wisconsin)

Essentially, the best USC can finish is 7-2 in Big Ten play and needs tiebreakers over five different teams — UCLA, Ohio State, Indiana, Northwestern and Nebraska — should those finish with the same record.
Big Ten standings for teams in the mix
*Teams that currently hold tiebreakers due to head-to-head wins
Simplifying the math, if USC wins out, UCLA's only loss comes to the Trojans and Riley's squad owns tiebreakers over any other remaining two-loss conference teams; they're in.

Riley's now 42-20 overall at USC and led the Trojans to an 11-win season in 2022 before the program entered the Big Ten. A potential playoff appearance, considering hard-to-stomach losses this fall against Oregon and Wisconsin, would make this campaign a raging success regardless of how the Big Ten standings shake out.

articles.headline: Forza co-creator Dan Greenawalt is reportedly leaving Microsoft
keyFacts: Dan Greenawalt is reportedly planning to retire from Microsoft after nearly 27 years, according to an internal memo cited by The Verge.
Greenawalt will stay on temporarily as an adviser during a changeover period, according to the memo from Playground Games' Trevor Williams.
The departure follows Microsoft's announcement in September to merge the Forza studios Turn 10 and Playground into one entity.
body: It's hard to overstate Dan's impact over the past 27 years. From shipping Project Gotham Racing on the original XBOX in 2001 to leading the creation of Forza, founding Turn 10 Studios and appearing so many times on our E3 stage, usually making a dramatic entrance with a supercar in tow—and so much more—we owe tremendous thanks and gratitude to Dan. On behalf of both teams, I would like to thank Dan for his leadership, his support, and his partnership. I wish him well for whatever comes next.

The Verge reports that Dan Greenawalt, studio head of Forza Motorsport developer Turn 10, is planning to retire after nearly 27 years, quoting an internal memo from Trevor Williams of Playground Games. "Dan Greenawalt has decided that this is the right time for him to retire from Microsoft," Williams is reported to have said, clarifying that Greenawalt will stay on temporarily as an adviser during a changeover period.

Microsoft announced in September that it plans to merge Turn 10 and Playground, the two Forza studios, into one entity as part of the same restructure that will merge Obsidian into Bethesda and hand Halo over to Activision. Oh, and that restructure will also see another 268 employees being laid off.

Turn 10 had already been turned into a support studio for Playground's Forza Horizon following the 2023 reboot of Forza Motorsport, with former developer Fred Russell saying last year that the Motorsport series died in a prior round of cuts at Microsoft.

He's written for Rock Paper Shotgun, The Big Issue, GamesRadar, Zam, Glixel, Five Out of Ten Magazine, and Playboy.com, whose cheques with the bunny logo made for fun conversations at the bank.
