articles.headline: Iran's supreme leader warns U.S., Israel against new attacks
keyFacts: Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei warned the U.S. and Israel against restarting military attacks amid heightened regional tensions.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the U.S. has not decided whether to resume strikes on Iran.
Mediators in Qatar are working to negotiate a peace deal between the U.S. and Iran.
body: What to know about the Iran war today:

- Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei warned the U.S. and Israel on Saturday against restarting the war amid weeks of heightened tensions and threats on both sides. He said there would be no geographical limitations for Iranian attacks if the war resumes.

- Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday no decision has been made yet on whether to restart military action against Iran, but "if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it and we have everything we need to be successful."
- President Trump said Friday the is "going to end soon," without specifying how, as Qatari mediators returned to Tehran to push for a peace deal being haggled over by Iran and the U.S.
Trump says U.S. still has "one or two" targets in Iran
President Trump said on Saturday that the United States has knocked out much of Iran's military but still has to "take care of" one or two targets, as Tehran warned of reprisals if attacked.
Mr. Trump maintained that negotiations with Iran to end the war, which was started by the U.S. and Israel in February, were "going fine but you know they're not very reliable."
The president said the U.S. is not in a hurry to take offensive action because it had already decimated Iran's military and nuclear program.
"We've knocked out their nuclear. We still have to take care of, I would say one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes," Mr. Trump told reporters at his Florida residence.
"You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain, and you have to take care of that. We can do that all very quickly," he added, referring to a suspected underground nuclear complex.
The Iranian government denied any nuclear work is carried out there.
Earlier Saturday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Mr. Trump has not made a decision about fresh strikes on Iran and that the U.S. would be open to a diplomatic solution.
Iran's top diplomat says proposal could reopen Strait of Hormuz in 2 days

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that a new proposal has been reached with mediators that would shorten the time to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz to two days. He said that Iranian diplomats were in Qatar for discussions.

Araghchi last month proposed reopening the waterway within a week if the U.S. agreed to lift its blockade of Iranian ports, release frozen Iranian assets and waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales, among other conditions. That was rejected.
In an interview with Qatar-based broadcaster Al Jazeera, Araghchi said that Iran isn't planning to meet with U.S. officials, but called recent U.S. efforts toward "broader dialogue" a positive step.
Araghchi said a decision on whether negotiations will be direct or indirect would be made "once Washington agrees to Iran's conditions."
U.S. blockade has redirected 144 ships in Strait of Hormuz, military says
The U.S. blockade on the Strait of Hormuz has now redirected 144 vessels, according to U.S. Central Command.
The U.S. had not provided an update on how many ships it had prevented from entering or exiting Iranian ports since exactly two weeks ago when it said it had redirected 138 vessels.
Earlier Saturday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had posted on X that the U.S. has taken out 1.5 billion barrels of oil without providing a timeframe.

Bessent posted that "transit levels are back to pre-conflict levels minus Iranian barrels." The U.S. has been guiding oil tankers out of the Persian Gulf under military escort over the past several months to do ship-to-ship oil transfers in the Gulf of Oman.
However, it's an expensive process and an open-ended mission at this point.
No changes to nuclear doctrine, but new attacks could necessitate change, Iranian official says

The powerful leader of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, who Vice President JD Vance engaged with a peace proposal last weekend, said on Saturday the country has not made any changes to its nuclear doctrine — but renewed strike might change that.

"No new decision has been made regarding changes to the nuclear doctrine," Secretary Mohsen Rezaei told official news outlet IRNA. "Of course, the discussion is raised that if war breaks out again, do we want to have the previous doctrine or not, but no new official and governmental decision has been made yet."

Iran has said many times the country was never attempting to enrich uranium to weapons grade, a claim largely disputed by the U.S. and Israel. President Trump has repeatedly made it known the main objective of the war in Iran is to prevent the country from ever acquiring a nuclear weapon.
Iran's nuclear sites have been hit repeatedly, both last summer in U.S. and Israeli strikes and in the renewed fighting this year, and it's unclear what capabilities remain.
Rezaei also told IRNA he has not yet responded to Vance's letter outlining some of the U.S. positions for peace talks.
Iran claims oil tanker hit mine, on fire east of the Strait of Hormuz
Iran has claimed another ship transiting the southern route of the Strait of Hormuz hit a mine and is on fire, according to semi-official Fars News Agency.

"This afternoon, a violating oil tanker that, disregarding warnings, was transiting in the prohibited and unsafe area in the east of the Strait of Hormuz, caught fire after striking sea mines," the country's navy said, according to Fars News Agency.
The news could not immediately be verified.

Iran has claimed nearly 10 ships have hit mines while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, specifically along the Omani coastline. That shipping lane is favored by the U.S. and is considered prohibited by Iran. Of the 81 attacks on ships in the strait since July 6, 59 of them have been on the southern route, according to the U.K. Marine Trade Operations Centre.
U.S. yet to decide whether it will restart strikes on Iran, Rubio says
President Trump has not made a decision about new strikes on Iran amid stalled peace talks, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday.

"We can achieve military objectives if we seek to. He hasn't made a decision. I have no announcement in that regard with you today, and nor do we take any of it lightly," Rubio said at a G20 press conference in Atlanta.
"If we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it and we have everything we need to be successful," Rubio added. "But we would prefer to do it peacefully."
He also would not characterize whether progress has been made in the last few days and said there is no timeframe on talks between the U.S. and Iran through its mediators.

Rubio continued to echo many of the things Mr. Trump has said in recent weeks and months. The United States' main objective is to prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon, and Rubio emphasized the threat to the rest of the world if they do.

"The Iranian regime is basically arguing is, 'Unless we get what we want, not only will we blow up ships, but we will destroy the energy infrastructure of our neighbors and the entire region.' Just think about that," Rubio said. "Because I think that we skip over that like that's some sort of normal behavior. That's not normal behavior, but we are there to help protect against it."
Iran targeted U.S. air defenses then hit aircraft and buildings on Mideast bases, AP analysis finds

Iran's strikes on more than two dozen U.S. bases in the Middle East focused on early warning systems before hitting aircraft and buildings, causing billions of dollars in equipment damage, according to an Associated Press analysis.

The AP independently verified damage to American targets using satellite imagery from multiple providers and spoke to four regional officials who were briefed or have firsthand knowledge of what was hit. The AP found that, through August, more than 115 drone or missile strikes claimed by Iran or Iranian-backed militias damaged or destroyed structures on 26 military bases and other sites with U.S. equipment.
The AP found that Iran initially focused its attacks on aircraft hangars and systems that detect incoming strikes, clearing the way for further strikes on warehouses, troop housing and more.

The damage has significantly reshaped the American foothold in the Middle East, with two regional officials saying the U.S. has moved many of its assets out of the Persian Gulf. That includes aircraft, air defense systems, communications systems and other equipment crucial to base operations, one of those officials said.

Most of the Iranian attacks have been in Kuwait, while U.S. sites in Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates also have been targeted, the analysis of satellite imagery shows.
Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait was struck at least 30 times, damaging or destroying at least 15 aircraft hangars, numerous warehouses and 10 buildings near a residential area.

Camp Buehring, also in Kuwait, faced even heavier losses. While Iranian attacks made most of its hangars inoperable, gathering places for troops sustained much more damage because the base had limited aircraft. Its gym was destroyed in March and a store for troops to buy products on the base was hit in late July.
Iran has no plans for talks with U.S., foreign minister says
Iran's top diplomat on Saturday said there were no plans to hold talks with the United States despite growing concerns over a return to war.

"Currently, there are no plans for meetings with American officials, and any speculation to the contrary is merely media assumption," Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in an interview with Al Jazeera, according to the state news agency IRNA.
"We see no need to meet with the Americans at present, our conditions are clear, and the mediators continue their consultations regarding them," Araghchi told Al Jazeera.

Qatari and Pakistani mediators met in Doha, Qatar, on Saturday, where an Iranian delegation was present. Iranian officials, through the Qatari mediators, received an outline for a peace deal from the U.S. last weekend, spearheaded by Vice President JD Vance.

"The American side's attempt to open the door to broader dialogue and understanding is considered a positive step, and if Washington's goal from Vance's message is to stir up differences, it will be a new mistake added to its previous errors," Araghchi told Al Jazeera on Saturday.
Regional leaders call for calm amid fears of new military escalation in Iran

Saudi Arabia's vice minister of foreign affairs said on Saturday the message from the region is that it wants a return to peace. Speaking at a security forum in Bahrain, Waleed ElKhereiji told the audience that efforts were being made to prevent a military escalation and reach an agreement to end the crisis with Iran.

"If you look at … the efforts that everybody is trying to do, the message is very clear. People in this part of the world want to bring peace back to the region," he said. But he said no one can predict the outcome of the efforts.

Concerns are rising about a return to all-out war, especially after Tuesday's midterm elections in the U.S. President Trump has opined during recent rallies that he could quickly bring the war to an end through military action.
Speaking at the same event, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said an escalation in the region would be extremely destructive.
"We are very confident that … the second round will be more dangerous, more destructive, and it will lead to nowhere," he said.
AP/CBS
Iran's supreme leader warns U.S. against resuming attacks
Iran's supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, on Saturday warned the United States against launching fresh attacks, amid weeks of heightened tensions and repeated threats.

"If the enemies once again launch military or terrorist attacks, it is the armed forces of the Islamic Republic and the Iranian nation that will determine the time and conditions for ending them," said a statement attributed to Khamenei posted on his Telegram channel.

The remarks came during a reported meeting between Khamenei and senior military commanders, including armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi, army chief Amir Hatami and Revolutionary Guards commander Ahmad Vahidi. It was the first reported meeting between them.
Khamenei has not been seen publicly since he became supreme leader, following his father Ayatollah Ali Khamenei's killing in U.S.-Israeli strikes at the start of the war in February.
According to the statement, Khamenei ordered the commanders to ensure that "any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response."
CBS/AFP
Saudi Arabia says it intercepted "hostile drone" in Riyadh region
Saudi air defences intercepted a drone in the Riyadh region on Saturday, according to the spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis.

"Air defences intercepted and destroyed a hostile drone in the Riyadh region," Turki al-Malki wrote on X, adding that "debris from the interception fell without causing injuries." Malki did not say who launched the drone.

In recent weeks, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis have ramped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, including by launching deadly strikes on Riyadh airport that forced its closure for two weeks and the cancellation of flagship events.
On Friday, Malki said the Houthis had targeted the Medina region, home to Islam's second holiest city, but the group later denied the claim.

The Houthi attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure, airports and ships come after hostilities resumed in Yemen over the summer between the Houthis and the country's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Riyadh.
More than 1,600 people have been killed and over 275,000 displaced since the fighting reignited, according to United Nations figures.
CBS/AFP
Supertanker caught fire after striking mine in Strait of Hormuz, Iran says

Iran's Revolutionary Guards said Friday that a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of oil struck a naval mine and caught fire while using an unauthorized route in the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian state media reported. The Guard said it was the fourth oil tanker to suffer an explosion Friday after attempting to use unauthorized routes through the strait.

Iran has repeatedly warned vessels against passing through the strait without Tehran's permission. It has claimed responsibility for attacks on ships and said last month that vessels attempting to pass through the strait without authorization would face "destruction." Tehran has asserted control over much of the waterway since the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Feb. 28.

Earlier on Friday, the Guard's navy said three other tankers caught fire after striking mines in the strait, Iranian state TV reported. It claimed the vessels had switched off their navigation and positioning systems and ignored repeated radio warnings. Iran's report did not identify the vessels or provide details about the crews. The Associated Press could not verify those claims.

Meanwhile, Oman said it had evacuated 25 crew members from a Panama-flagged tanker that was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz, 1.6 nautical miles off the coast of Musandam Governorate, catching fire. It is unclear whether that incident is related to the fires described by Iran.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center also reported Friday that a vessel was struck by an "unknown projectile" south of Lavan, an island just off mainland Iran near Shidvar. The organization, part of the British military that monitors maritime safety, said the crew was safe.
Strikes blamed on Houthis target Yemen presidential palace

Yemen's Houthis targeted the presidential palace in Aden on Friday with two missiles, a police official told AFP, hours after Saudi forces said they had intercepted an attack by the group on the Gulf kingdom.
Aden, the seat of Yemen's Saudi-backed and internationally recognized government, has been targeted repeatedly since Yemen's dormant civil war reignited in July.

Two eyewitnesses told AFP they saw ambulances entering the palace in Aden, a large compound made up of several buildings including facilities used by government and Saudi-led coalition forces, after the incident.
Shortly before, residents and an AFP journalist said they heard two blasts in the city.
The Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa to the north, most recently struck the perimeter of Aden's airport on Wednesday after saying they had targeted a naval base and a military camp last week.
October marks record high for reported strikes in Strait of Hormuz, U.K. navy says

There were more strikes reported in and around the Strait of Hormuz than any other month during the Iran-U.S. war, according to the U.K. Marine Trade Operations Centre, which is supported by the Royal Navy.

There were just over 30 attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, Gulf of Oman or Persian Gulf reported in October, with only March, the first month of the war, reporting even 30 attacks, according to the UKMTO. There were twice as many attacks in October as there were in September. While there were likely more attacks in the month, the UKMTO only counts attacks reported by verified vessels in the region.

The war also crossed the eight-month mark this week as it started on Feb. 28. Since the war started, there have been 145 reported incidents, the UKMTO said. While the UKMTO does not track who fired the projectiles that hit vessels, the vast majority of strikes came via Iran. Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps often claims responsibility for the attacks.
Iran has started to claim a large number of ships hitting mines in the region as well, though they largely do not appear on the list of incidents from the UKMTO.

Since July 6, 59 of the 81 projectile strikes on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz region came along the southern route, the UKMTO said. The U.S. has championed the southern route, and used it to escort oil tankers out of the Persian Gulf, while Iran calls the route illegal and says ships need to travel north, along the Iranian coast.
Rubio hosts G20 ministers as Iran, Ukraine wars divide members

Secretary of State Marco Rubio opened talks Friday with G20 counterparts including Russia's Sergei Lavrov, in meetings set to be fractious as wars in Ukraine and Iran, alongside surging energy costs, fan discord.
The foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta takes place just days before crucial midterm elections, setting the stage for a December G20 leaders' summit in Miami at President Trump's Doral resort.
But ongoing conflicts have deepened rifts even as the United States seeks to focus on economic growth, trade imbalances and supply chain challenges in areas like energy and critical minerals.
Rubio warned at an opening plenary session that the world faces "interconnected economic and geopolitical crises, many of which pose severe threats" to the global economy.
He urged the G20 to work together against threats including strains to global energy and food supply chains, and on freedom of navigation.

Still, few breakthroughs are expected this week from the Group of 20 economies — which include China, India, Russia, Japan, Germany and France — as officials face divisions over Moscow's war on Ukraine and fallout from the conflict with Iran.
Global energy prices have rocketed since U.S.-Israel strikes on Iran from late February triggered Tehran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

"This is the last test case the G20 has, at least under the US G20 presidency, until Miami," Alisha Chhangani of the Atlantic Council told AFP. Its outcomes will affect how the December summit shapes up.
UAE says oil spill from tanker in Strait of Hormuz has been contained

No new oil leakage has been detected from the tanker GEM NO. 2 following an in the United Arab Emirates' territorial waters, as cleanup operations continue along the UAE coastline, the Persian Gulf nation's official WAM news agency reported.

WAM quoted the Ministry of Energy and Infrastructure as saying Friday that technical teams had repaired damaged parts of the vessel, restored some operating systems and assessed the ship's structural integrity. Authorities said the source of the spill had been stopped.
According to the Ministry of Climate Change and Environment, the oil slick is concentrated off Umm Al-Quwain, extending toward coastal areas of Ras Al Khaimah, Ajman and Sharjah.
Pollution levels have declined, while monitoring and cleanup operations continue.

The British maritime security agency UKMTO reported on Oct. 9 that a vessel had been hit by a projectile off the UAE coast, causing a fire that was later brought under control. It did not assign blame, but Iran has repeatedly targeted commercial ships in and around the southern Strait of Hormuz, which includes the UAE coastline.
Saudis intercept drone, missile allegedly launched by Houthis
The Saudis intercepted a drone near the capital of Riyadh on Friday afternoon as well as a ballistic missile in southern Saudi Arabia, according to the country's Coalition Joint Forces Command.
The coalition said both were fired by the Houthis. It's unclear exactly where the missile was intercepted in southern Saudi Arabia.

The Houthis have regularly targeted locations in Saudi Arabia, everywhere from just over the border from Yemen to hundreds of miles into the interior, including Riyadh. Airports have been a consistent target of Houthi attacks.
The Saudi coalition had earlier announced it intercepted a drone near the holy city of Mecca, which the Houthis denied was fired by their forces.
Lebanon charges 13 people over seized shipment of Hezbollah explosives

A Lebanese military court on Friday charged 13 people for their alleged involvement in shipping explosives to Hezbollah, a judicial source told the AFP news agency, after authorities seized the roughly 1,100-pound cargo earlier this month.

The charges come as pressure mounts on Hezbollah, long a major political and paramilitary force in Lebanon that the U.S. and Israel consider an Iran-backed terrorist organization. The group has been weakened by back-to-back wars with Israel and is now facing a concerted push from authorities in Beirut, with backing from the Trump administration, to disarm its military wing.
Only two of the 13 people charged over the explosives shipment have been detained, and only eight have been identified, with the remaining five known only by noms de guerre.

Proceedings have been opened "against 12 members of Hezbollah, and one of their spouses," a judicial official told AFP. They were charged with "violating government decisions, possession of arms and explosives, and criminal conspiracy to undermine the authority of the state," the source said.
In a rare admission, Hezbollah acknowledged ownership of the vehicle and its cargo, and even demanded the shipment be returned.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has vowed that authorities "will deal with weapons outside the legal framework with the required firmness."

In June, Lebanon and Israel that included the disarmament of Hezbollah and a gradual Israeli withdrawal from occupied territory in southern Lebanon, with the Lebanese army stepping in to secure the area.

So far, Hezbollah has flatly refused to disarm or acknowledge the ceasefire, and very little of what Israel calls its occupied "security zone" in southern Lebanon has been handed over to Lebanese forces.
CBS/AFP
Oman evacuates 25 crew members from vessels burning off its Strait of Hormuz coast
Oman's navy has evacuated 25 crew members from a Panama-flagged commercial vessel after it was targeted and a fire broke out on board, the Omani Maritime Security Center said in a statement Friday.

The evacuation was carried out in coordination with the Maritime Security Center approximately 1.6 nautical miles off the coast of Musandam Governorate, the northern tip of Oman that juts out into the center of the Strait of Hormuz.
Crew members were "provided with the necessary medical care," the navy said in a statement.

Earlier Friday, Iran's navy and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said two ships were on fire after striking sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz after attempting to use shipping lanes close to Oman's coast that the U.S. military insists are safe and open, but Tehran considers illegal.
ExxonMobil profits double to $15.4 billion on oil price surge

Major U.S. oil and gas giant ExxonMobil reported Friday that its third-quarter profits had more than doubled to $15.4 billion, as it benefited from higher oil prices and refining margins due to the U.S.-Iran war.
Profits in the period were slightly more than double the $7.5 billion in the year-ago period.
Oil prices have been high since the start of the war. As of Friday, the two main benchmark products, Brent crude and U.S. West Texas Intermediate, remained up about 70% compared to a year ago.
CBS/AFP
Iranian navy claims "enemy drone" destroyed, 2 oil tankers on fire in Hormuz strait
The Iranian navy said Friday that an enemy drone was "struck and destroyed" east of the Strait of Hormuz.

In a statement, the navy also said two oil tankers "were damaged and caught fire after striking naval mines," accusing the vessels of ignoring warnings and navigating in prohibited and unsafe waters with their tracking systems switched off.
It was not immediately clear if the two vessels referred to by the Iranian navy were the same tankers that Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps in the strait.
President Trump says Iran war "going to get wrapped up soon"
President Donald Trump said Friday that the war with Iran is "going to get wrapped up soon."
Speaking to Kansas City radio station KCMO ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, the president said "it's going to get wrapped up soon," without specifying how.
"We need a guarantee there'll never be a nuclear weapon," he added.
U.S. CENTCOM chief renews insistence that Iran's navy is destroyed and Strait of Hormuz shipping lanes are open

The commander of the U.S. military's Central Command, Adm. Brad Cooper, reiterated his longstanding assertions on Friday that Iran's navy is "at the bottom of the sea" and that southern commercial shipping lanes through the Strait of Hormuz are clear of Iranian mines and safe to navigate.

In a video posted on social media, Cooper said the U.S. had helped Gulf partners export more than 1.5 billion barrels of crude oil since the summer, while the U.S. naval blockade had prevented Iran from exporting any oil through the strait.
Cooper said he had recently flown over the strait and seen U.S. military "assets in the air and on the water."

"What I didn't see," said Cooper, was Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps "out there at all. They patrolled the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters for decades, harassing and threatening and seizing commercial vessels at will, but they were not out there because Iran's navy is all at the bottom of the sea."

Cooper renewed the claim made by President Trump and the Pentagon since late August that "we also successfully cleared the strait's internationally recognized primary transit routes of Iranian sea mines. And today, U.S. forces remain highly vigilant and present to ensure that all primary transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz remain free and clear."

His comments came a day after Iran's navy claimed four vessels had struck sea mines and been disabled as the attempted to transit the strait via the U.S.-backed southern route. The U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center said Thursday evening, meanwhile, that a tanker was struck by a projectile in the strait.
It was unclear if the ship reported by UKMTO to have been hit was one of the four Iran said had hit mines.
Source confirms to CBS News Qatari mediators are in Iran to convey tweaks to latest peace proposal
A source familiar with the ongoing diplomacy confirmed to CBS News that Qatari mediators were in Tehran on Friday to convey the latest edits to a draft proposal to end the U.S. war with Iran.
The source said there were indications of progress being made.

A draft was presented by Qatari mediators last Sunday, and a response from Iran is expected by the weekend. The aim of the proposal is to avert a return to U.S. military action against Iran, which President Trump has threatened multiple times in recent weeks.
Iran says 2 tankers on "unauthorized route" in Strait of Hormuz had "incidents and were brought to a halt"

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Friday that two oil tankers had been halted after unspecified "incidents" as they attempted to transit what Tehran considers an unauthorized route through the Strait of Hormuz.

"Two offending oil tankers, one in the eastern part and the other in the western part of the Strait of Hormuz, which were attempting to pass through the unauthorized route, encountered incidents and were brought to a halt in the waters south of the strait," the IRGC said in a statement.
Iran has repeatedly warned shippers that using the southern route through the waterway, which has been promoted by the U.S., puts them at risk as the regime deems it an illegal passage.

The tankers had "switched off all their navigation and positioning systems and, with the support of the terrorist U.S. military, were attempting to exit through the unauthorized route," the IRGC statement said.
The IRGC did not specify the nature of the incidents, which came a day after Iran's armed forces said at least four tankers had been forced to stop in the area after hitting sea mines.

The U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center said Thursday evening that a tanker was struck by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz. It was unclear if the ship reported by UKMTO to have been hit was one of the four Iran said had hit mines, but the timing of the report suggested it could have been a separate incident.
CBS/AFP
Qatari officials return to Iran to push for peace deal with U.S.
Qatari officials returned to Iran on Friday to push for a peace deal between Tehran and Washington, Iran's state-run IRNA news agency, along with Reuters and AFP, reported.
The talks have been coordinated with the U.S., an official told Reuters.

The delegation is led by a senior adviser to Qatar's prime minister and foreign minister and is scheduled to meet with senior Iranian officials, IRNA said, adding that the discussions would focus on bilateral relations between Iran and Qatar, as well as developments in the region.

An official briefed on the latest diplomacy confirmed to CBS News Wednesday that Qatari mediators had presented Iran with a new draft deal to end the war. A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Qatar had , and that Tehran would not change its stance on the nuclear issue, something Washington wants included in negotiations from the start.
Tehran wants the U.S. to first lift its blockade of Iranian ports and to drop sanctions limiting the country's gas and oil sales.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday in a post on X that Tehran "continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed" and is working with mediators to review ideas that Tehran included in a proposal floated last month, which was summarily rejected by President Trump but which Iran still wants to see used as the basis for a new ceasefire agreement.

On Thursday, Mr. Trump said a letter from Vice President JD Vance to Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei — which was reported by multiple outlets as an attempt to restart peace negotiations — was an outreach intended only to help get medical supplies into Iran.
Iran has yet to reply to the letter, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.
U.S. military death toll since start of Iran war rises to 23, Pentagon says

The U.S. Department of Defense has added two more service member deaths to its official account of casualties since the war with Iran started more than eight months ago, bringing the overall death toll to 23.

Both of the newly noted deaths on the Defense Casualty Analysis System portal were noncombat related. In total the DCAS portal says 11 service members have been killed by enemy fire during the war, and 12 others have died under circumstances deemed nonhostile, which includes accidents and sickness.

Both of the service members recently added as nonhostile deaths were airmen, including one who died of an illness and another from unspecified causes that remain under investigation, The Washington Post quoted the Air Force as saying.

The two deaths added to the DCAS system are listed under Overseas Operations, which includes deaths recorded by the Pentagon after it for the offensive against Iran in May, after Secretary of State Marco Rubio declared the operation over.
Saudi coalition says Houthi drone intercepted in Mecca region
The Saudi-led coalition said Friday that it had intercepted and destroyed a drone in the Mecca region fired by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
"A drone launched by the terrorist Houthi militia has been intercepted and destroyed in the Mecca region," the coalition wrote in a post on X.
The Houthis denied any attempt to strike Saudi Arabia on Friday, the Reuters news agency reported.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said on social media that the group hadn't conducted any operations aimed at Saudi territory, adding that the Houthis only target Saudi oil facilities and military bases.
CBS/AFP
Tanker struck by projectile in Strait of Hormuz, U.K. navy says, as Iran claims four ships hit sea mines

A tanker was struck Thursday evening by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center reported, after Iran's navy claimed four ships had struck sea mines in the area.
UKMTO said the ship hit by a projectile was exiting the strait along the southern route, which the U.S. has encouraged international shipping companies to use, when it came under fire.
"There are no reported injuries to the crew or environmental impact … at this time," UKMTO said.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and its military claimed in two separate announcements earlier Thursday that four tankers had struck sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz, causing fires.

It was unclear if the ship reported by UKMTO to have been struck by a projectile was one of the four Iran said had hit mines, but the timing of the report from the maritime monitor suggested it could have been a separate incident.
Iran has not yet responded to letter from Vance, Iranian media says

Iran has not yet responded to a letter sent by Vice President JD Vance to the secretary of the Iranian Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, according to the semi-official Tasnim News agency, which is closely affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

Tasnim said in a Thursday post on its official Telegram social media account that Tehran was not prepared to drop any of its core conditions for a ceasefire, which include lifting the American blockade of Iran's ports, easing sanctions and giving Iran access to its frozen financial assets held abroad, among other things.

Multiple news outlets have reported that Vance's letter to Rezaei was an attempt to restart peace negotiations, but President Trump said Wednesday that it was a focused outreach intended only to help get medical supplies into Iran.

articles.headline: Trump grants visa to mother of Ghanaian boy killed in NYC — Mamdani
keyFacts: US President Donald Trump agreed to grant a visa to the mother of Javits Frimpong, a 15-year-old boy killed in the Bronx, according to Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
Frimpong was shot in the abdomen on his way to school on Thursday and later died in the hospital, police stated.
Police reported that no arrests have been made and the investigation into the shooting is ongoing.
body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Saturday that US President Donald Trump had agreed to grant a visa to the mother of a 15-year-old boy who was killed in a neighborhood in Bronx earlier this week.
Javits Frimpong moved to New York from Ghana last year to be with his father and begin a new life in the US, according to Representative Ritchie Torres, a Democrat from the Bronx.
Frimpong was shot in the abdomen on Thursday morning on his way to school and later died in the hospital, according to New York City police.
There have been no arrests in the case so far, with police investigating the shooting.
Mamdani says he spoke to Trump
"I just got off the phone with President Trump and he has agreed to grant her visa immediately," Mamdani posted on X.
"The murder of a child is a pain no parent should have to endure, let alone from thousands of miles away," he wrote. "Javits Frimpong's mother deserves to say goodbye to her son in person."
The killing led to an outpouring of grief in New York, with Torres writing, "Our entire borough is mourning a young man who should have had his whole future ahead of him."
The White House is yet to comment on the Trump-Mamdani phone call.
Teen was bullied in school, father says
Thomas Frimpong remembered his son as a quiet boy and said he was bullied in school by two boys.
Ghana's Foreign Minister Sam Okudzeto Ablakwa also thanked Mamdani and Trump in a post on X.
He said Ghanaian officials were coordinating with Javits Frimpong's mother to assist her with the visa application process.

articles.headline: Trump on Iran negotiations: ‘We’re not in that much of a hurry’
keyFacts: President Donald Trump said the United States is not in a hurry to sign a deal with Iran.
Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei said an unrestricted response would follow any U.S. or Israeli attacks.
Trump indicated potential future military action against Iran could occur after the midterm elections.
body: President Donald Trump said on Saturday night the United States is not “in that much of a hurry” to sign a negotiated deal with Iran as the president weighs launching a fresh wave of strikes against the terrorist-sponsoring nation following the midterm elections .

When asked if there’s a “timeframe for the Qatari-mediated negotiations” while fielding questions from reporters at a Halloween event at Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach, Florida, Trump said there’s no rush to strike a deal since Iran’s navy, air force, and anti-aircraft equipment have been “knocked out.”

“We’ve knocked out almost every piece of military equipment they have,” he said. “We’ve knocked out a lot of their manufacturing capability. We’ve knocked out their nuclear. We still have to take care of, I would say, one or two sites. But we can do that in ten minutes. And we have that planned.”

Trump’s comments come the same day that Iranian leadership heightened its rhetoric against the U.S., as Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei said an “immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response” would follow any American or Israeli threat of new attacks. The last confirmed strikes against Iran occurred in August.

“With all informational capacity, we monitor the enemy’s movements and preparations and update the target bank,” Major Gen. Ali Abdollahi, the chief of staff of the armed forces of Iran, said on Saturday as well. “Whenever signs of hostile enemy action are confirmed, the armed forces will not wait for the start of his action in choosing the time and manner of response.”
IRANIAN SUPREME LEADER VOWS ‘UNRESTRICTED RESPONSE’ TO ANY US OR ISRAELI STRIKES

Trump offered a glimpse into what potential action may look like once the midterm elections are over, saying, “You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain; you have to take care of that. We could do that all very quickly.” Trump also said last week the conflict would be over “very soon.”

Trump has stood by his February decision to strike Iran despite the public’s broadly unfavorable view of the conflict, and the belief that disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz may be linked to stubbornly high inflation. Though Trump largely ran on lowering costs during the 2024 presidential election, many Republican figures fear the issue of “affordability” may sink the GOP’s chances of retaining control of Congress on Tuesday.

articles.headline: Trump pleads for voters to pick Blakeman to save New York from ‘worst governor’
keyFacts: Donald Trump urged voters during a tele-rally to elect Republican Bruce Blakeman as New York governor over incumbent Democrat Kathy Hochul.
Polls show Hochul leading Blakeman by 11 to 14 points, while her spokesperson criticized Blakeman's alignment with Trump.
Trump stated he expects Blakeman to win and promised tremendous federal help if Blakeman is elected.
body: President Donald Trump on Saturday made a last-minute plea to New Yorkers to vote for Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman on Election Day, saying the Nassau County executive can save the Empire State from Gov. Kathy Hochul’s “failed and incompetent” leadership.

“Kathy Hochul may be the worst governor in the history of New York State and one of the worst in the nation,” roared the commander-in-chief during a tele-rally promoting the campaigns of Blakeman and two other New York Republicans, Attorney General candidate Saritha Komatireddy and upstate congressional hopeful Anthony Constantino.
“She been a disaster, and I can tell you that Bruce has been a friend of mine for a long time,” Trump added.

“Anybody that can do what he did in politics and get resounding results, and not only that, he has the safest county in the United States of America [according to US News & World Report] … He’s a great manager.”
Despite recent polls showing Hochul ahead anywhere from 11 to 14 points, Trump said he expects the Nassau County executive to win.

“I’ll be waiting for his call,” the president said. “I bet he’s going to be one of the first calls if he wins, and he’ll get tremendous help from the federal government. And it’s hard to help people that do such a bad job. It’s almost like throwing good money after bad.”
Hochul spokesperson Ryan Radulovack responded by attempting to paint Trump as a boogeyman, something the governor has also done many times throughout the campaign.
“Blakeman … started with the promise to ‘bring Trump-style leadership to Albany,’ and his closing message is telling people how little he regrets going full Trump in this campaign,” added Radulovack.
“Gov. Hochul has put money back in New Yorkers’ pockets, invested $4 billion in public safety, and fought back against Trump’s attacks,” while Blakeman “defends everything Trump does.”
Trump during the tele-rally also found some time to claim that the war with Iran is all but over.
“We’re winning very easily the war with Iran,” Trump said.

articles.headline: Gabby Williams powers Valkyries past Dream in Game 7 for historic WNBA title
keyFacts: Gabby Williams scored 30 points to lead the second-year Golden State Valkyries to a 68-63 victory over the Atlanta Dream in Game 7.
The victory secured the first championship in franchise history for the Valkyries and marked the first-ever Game 7 in WNBA history.
Golden State claimed the title after winning Games 1, 4, and 5 before clinching the series on their home court.
body: In the middle of Chase Center, the Golden State Valkyries gathered somewhere they have been only a handful of times. They are, after all, just a second-year franchise.
But on Saturday night they came together to collect their trophy as WNBA champions. Kaila Charles embraced Tiffany Hayes as they jumped up and down. Kayla Thornton screamed towards the ceiling.
Teams are not supposed to do this so fast, but the Valkyries did.
Gabby Williams scored 30 points, most of them coming in a second-half tear in which she carried the Valkyries to a 68-63 win over the Atlanta Dream in Game 7 of the WNBA finals.

It is the first championship in franchise history for the Valkyries, who began play just two seasons ago. They beat Dallas in the first round and swept the defending champion Las Vegas Aces to reach the finals before prevailing in an intense, seven-game slugfest against Atlanta.
It was also the first-ever Game 7 in WNBA history. The league expanded the finals to a best-of-seven format last year, but Las Vegas swept Phoenix in four games.

The Valkyries led 14-12 after the first quarter on Saturday, thanks in large part to an 8-0 run to open the game. Golden State recorded five blocks before the Dream made their first field goal, but Atlanta responded with a 7-0 run to briefly take the lead.

The second quarter, though, was a reversal of the first. Golden State did not make a field goal until three minutes remained in the period, while the Dream went on a 9-0 run. The Valkyries had missed their first 10 three-point attempts before Thornton finally connected from beyond the arc in the second.

After Golden State had struggled from long range all game, Williams hit three consecutive three-pointers in the third quarter to cut Atlanta’s lead to two. The Valkyries led 45-44 entering the fourth, largely thanks to Williams’s 15 points in the period.
Allisha Gray hit a mid-range jumper to tie the score at 53 with 4min 52sec remaining, but the Valkyries retook the lead a minute and a half later on a Williams free throw.
From there, the teams traded blows in a finish that mirrored the back-and-forth nature of the series.
Williams gave Golden State a 60-57 lead with 2min 14sec remaining on a contested three-pointer with two seconds left on the shot clock, and the Dream never recovered.

Golden State won Games 1, 4 and 5 before clinching the series in Game 7 on their home court. The Valkyries entered the postseason as the No 2 seed and enjoyed home-court advantage throughout the playoffs.

Hayes scored 11 points en route to her first WNBA title at the age of 37, while point guard Veronica Burton added 10 points and 10 rebounds for a double-double. For Atlanta, Jordin Canada scored 18 points, Gray added 16 and Angel Reese was held to eight points and 12 rebounds.

articles.headline: Data centers are now a midterm issue, even in Brooklyn
keyFacts: AI and data centers dominated discussions at a recent New York midterm election event hosted by Newsreel, according to the article.
Data Center Watch reported that nearly $200 billion in data center projects were delayed or blocked in early 2026 due to political and community opposition.
Founder Jack Brewster stated that AI has become an election issue for regular voters, focusing on feelings of replacement in rural areas and wealth distribution in places like Brooklyn.
body: On Thursday evening, I slipped on my neon yellow heels and a floral mini dress. It’s New York, so I can wear whatever I want to a midterm election event full of media types, techies, policy advocates, and, well, does anyone else even exist at these things? I walked into the dimly blue-lit Brooklyn warehouse and was surprised to see the room already filling up.

Newsreel, the media company founded by former Forbes and Newsweek reporter Jack Brewster, hosted the event, and the lineup was heavy-hitting. Kenneth Schlenker, co-founder of the focus app Opal, sat down for a fireside chat about “the state of attention,” and Aryan Banjan, who built the campaign management software Barza, gave a midterm forecast. I, meanwhile, was moderating a panel on data centers.
Brewster said the goal was for people to “put their phones away and talk to each other about the election, five days out.”
As the evening progressed, however, one topic consumed nearly every conversation: AI, data centers, and the backlash against the growing technocracy.

Lately, as a tech reporter, I’ve noticed a growing chasm between tech and everyone else. I spend most of my days talking to people who see the benefits of AI, who are so ambitious in building it and so optimistic that it will succeed that, when I talk to people beyond the tech world, I forget how ugly it all seems to them. Outside the tech bubble, data centers and AI have become such an intense ballot-box issue that they could sway some midterm races on November 3.

A recent report from Data Center Watch found that almost $200 billion in data center projects were delayed, stalled, or blocked in the first half of 2026 due to political and community opposition. Meanwhile, states like Pennsylvania, Georgia, Texas, New York, and Virginia are considering more guardrails and transparency around data centers’ rapid development. Hundreds of new data centers are planned in Virginia alone, a state already nicknamed the “data center capital of the world.”

A fireside chat with New York City Council member Chi Ossé, just before my panel, set the tone. AI came up near the end; Ossé said he doesn’t really use it. To me, though, he didn’t seem to be for or against it. He mostly emphasized that he would like to see tech executives held more accountable and trillionaires like Elon Musk taxed more. He described himself as a democratic socialist, but a “law and order” one. When CEOs talk about a technology that could deplete 10% of human civilization, he said, “they should be called to testify in front of Congress.”

My panel was up next. I moderated a discussion with Maia Woluchem, a technology and human rights researcher, and Hilary Flint, an environmental and public health advocate, about data centers. As I took the stage, I decided to get a better read on the crowd. I asked, “Who here is pro-AI data center?” and was promptly booed. Our conversation covered a range of topics and emotions. People are upset that big tech companies appear to be cutting secret deals with local officials to build billion-dollar data centers. In some cases, zoning rules make it unclear what is being built until it’s too late to protest.

At the same time, people are struggling with the cost of living and doing everything they can to hold onto what’s left of the American Dream, while tech leaders talk about AI replacing workers, or even humanity itself. Residents feel they have lost control over what happens in their communities, and they worry about the environmental and health risks. The panel agreed that data centers are the physical embodiment of people’s fears and anger toward the tech class and the rapid pace of technology.

“What is a life worth?” Flint said when I brought up the benefits that some communities have seen from data center build-outs. People still protest, she said, because they “value their lives a little bit more than a temporary check.”

The panel after mine featured NewsNation host Batya Ungar-Sargon; political strategist Morris Katz, who worked on Zohran Mamdani’s campaign; and Vox’s Astead Herndon. They were supposed to be talking about the future of the Democratic Party. But once again, the conversation shifted to data centers. Ungar-Sargon noted that some labor unions support data centers because of the jobs they promise. (Reports show that data centers create many jobs initially, but those jobs are not permanent once construction ends.)

“There used to be a lot of pride in a community in the Rust Belt about very ugly, enormous buildings in their communities because everybody worked there,” she said, nodding to an earlier comment I’d made about data centers being ugly. “And they knew that building represented prosperity for themselves, stability for their children, and a future and a piece of the American dream.”

Herndon noted that Vivek Ramaswamy was booed for making a similar point in Ohio, a Rust Belt state. “I just want to reinforce the lack of consent happening,” he said. “Because that’s true among Republicans in those places and I’ve watched it.” Katz was also skeptical. “It’s the same people who have taken so many union jobs away,” he said. “The same institutional powers that have robbed labor and working people of jobs and profit. Now coming back to essentially finish the job and take whatever scraps remain.”
Along the warehouse walls, I noticed sticky notes answering posted questions, including “Will we ever be able to get Big Money out of politics?” “God, I hope so,” one note said.

People rushed the bar when the panel ended, and techno music began to blast. They broke into small groups, where AI and data centers were once again the topic, this time in more private conversations. I asked Brewster if he was surprised by how much of the conversation focused on AI and data centers.

“It came up in every conversation on stage, and it was the second most common topic in the questions people sent us when they RSVP’d,” he said, adding that it was happening even in New York, where data centers aren’t very visible. “AI has become an election issue for regular voters,” he said. “In rural communities, the backlash is about feeling replaced. In a place like Brooklyn, it’s more about who gets rich from it.”

Before leaving, I made the rounds, asking people to name the craziest thing they’d seen in tech this year. Two tech founders mentioned the AI assistant startup Instinct, while a non-tech person named Sam Altman

Another non-tech person brought up the rise of deepfakes and AI art. AI art, she said, is starting to signal cheapness. That may be why luxury brands are going the other way: Prada’s holiday campaign features hand-drawn illustrations, and Hermès has been spotlighting artists’ handmade work on Instagram.

On my way out, I spoke to a software engineer who said the craziest thing she’d seen this year was a person who painted their nails orange for Halloween and was asked if it was a tribute to the Anthropic IPO. I admitted that I, too, had once worn a burnt orange dress and briefly thought of myself as the Claude logo.

She later told me data centers are popping up in her Southern California hometown, too. Hearing that, I thought for the first time about how I’d feel if one popped up in mine. She grew up in a Chinese immigrant community, where neighbors are putting signs in their yards showing dragons choking a data center.
The signs have since been translated into other languages, she said.

articles.headline: Trump to grant visa to mother of teen killed in Bronx shooting, Mamdani says
keyFacts: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said President Donald Trump agreed to immediately grant a visa to the mother of a slain Bronx teenager.
Police said 15-year-old Javits Frimpong was shot and killed while going to school, and detectives are currently looking for three teenagers.
Ghanaian Foreign Minister Sam Okudzeto Ablakwa said the Foreign Ministry will work with US authorities to secure justice.
body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said on Saturday that President Donald Trump agreed to grant a visa to the mother of a teenager who was shot and killed in the Bronx on Thursday.

15-year-old Javits Frimpong, who moved from Ghana to live with his father roughly a year ago, was shot in the abdomen on Thursday morning while going to his school near Crotona Park. He died later that day at St. Barnabas Hospital, police said.

“The murder of a child is a pain no parent should have to endure, let alone from thousands of miles away,” Mamdani said. “Javits Frimpong’s mother deserves to say goodbye to her son in person. I just got off the phone with President Trump and he has agreed to grant her visa immediately. All of New York City is mourning this tragedy.”

Frimpong’s story began circulating late in the week after his father, Thomas, candidly spoke to local reporters about his son’s death. A taxi driver, he said he’s lived in the United States for two decades and makes trips often back to Ghana to visit his wife and the late teenager’s mother.

Detectives are looking for three teenagers in connection with the shooting, according to CBS News . Frimpong’s father had said two boys were recently suspended from the school for bullying his son. No arrests have been made and the incident remains under investigation.

“Every child in the Bronx deserves to walk to school without fearing for their life,” Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-NY) said. “And no parent should have to endure what Javits’s father, Thomas, is enduring now. My heart is with him and with everyone in Claremont grieving today.”
WOMAN IN CUSTODY AFTER ALLEGEDLY SHOOTING A BYSTANDER NEAR REPUBLICAN PARTY HQ IN VIRGINIA

A vigil was held Friday night to honor Frimpong’s life, which was attended by religious leaders, community members, and family members of other teenagers who have lost their lives to violence in New York City. The New York City Department of Education offered counseling and other support to students and staff of the school Frimpong attended, Dreamyard Preparatory School.

Foreign Minister Sam Okudzeto Ablakwa said on Friday he had spoken with Frimpong’s father and “directly conveyed the condolences of the Government and people of Ghana.” He also said the Foreign Ministry will “work tirelessly with US authorities to ensure justice is secured.”

articles.headline: These firms you've never heard of are feeding fears the AI bubble could burst
keyFacts: Neocloud firms lease high-powered computers to major AI developers, but analysts and investors have raised concerns about their heavy debt loads.
Stock prices for neocloud firms like CoreWeave and Nebius have dropped significantly over the past month amid growing financial worries.
Industry analysts predict that many neocloud firms face consolidation or acquisition as borrowing costs rise and their financial risks increase.
body: - Published
A once-obscure corner of the AI ecosystem finds itself in the spotlight â and investors don't all like what they see.
Names like CoreWeave and Nebius are familiar to the tech set in San Francisco and Silicon Valley.
These data centre companies, known as neocloud firms, run large warehouses packed with expensive computers, which they lease to major AI developers like Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta.
They're now the subject of one of Silicon Valley's most heated debates.
Many question whether neocloud firms are financially sound and what their recent stumbles tell us about the state of the AI economy.

Analysts at Gartner predict by 2030, 80% of neocloud firms will "cease independent operations", while Forrester's experts expect at least three of them to be imminently acquired "as finances get shaky".
On Thursday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent tried to downplay recent concerns about neocloud firms, calling them "a small component of the overall ecosystem, external" on CNBC.
Debt worries
Neocloud firms often finance themselves by signing long-term lease contracts with major tech customers who need quick access to computing power.
Firms can then borrow money using those contracts â plus the AI chips they purchase â as collateral, explained analyst Cory Johnson of "The Quiet Period" IPO research outfit.
He said debt is common across neocloud firms because the hardware has to be paid for up front.
Take the industry leader: CoreWeave. It's a fraction of the size of some of the Big Tech companies it serves.
But Johnson believes lenders sometimes consider the creditworthiness of CoreWeave's customers, like Microsoft or Meta, more than the company's when they lend.
"This helps explain how CoreWeave accumulated $35.1bn (Â£26.3bn) in debt," he said.
Some jittery investors appear to be having second thoughts.
CoreWeave stock has lost a quarter of its value over the past month, and it's not alone.
Shares in other neocloud firms like Nebius, IREN, and Applied Digital have all shed about that much if not more during the same period.
Debt investors also appear spooked, and are demanding ever-higher returns from several firms in the sector.

CoreWeave's CEO Mike Intrator has said that the market is acting "irrationally" and has expressed confidence in its business model. Some of the world's most consequential companies are queuing up for CoreWeave's infrastructure and other AI services.
Origins in crypto
Several neocloud firms have their roots in the volatile crypto mining industry, made of companies that generate cryptocurrencies, like Bitcoin.
Crypto miners use some of the same kind of physical infrastructure that is used to develop AI.
CoreWeave was founded in 2017 with a focus on mining Ethereum.
IREN, Core Scientific and Applied Digital also started in crypto mining.
Their infrastructure left them well-positioned when AI exploded in 2022 with the introduction of OpenAI's ChatGPT.
One outlier is Nebius, which was known as Yandex NV when it was part of Russia's version of Google before splitting off and changing its name in 2024.
Now, the success of these firms hinges on the fate of major AI developers and hyperscalers â even larger data centre operators which neocloud firms often count as key customers.
"There is just an enormous amount of spending getting injected into the system," said Melissa Otto, head of Visible Alpha Research at S&P Global. "It's an arms race."
And neoclouds have benefitted.
But the trade-off of their model is "greater financial risk" in the face of change, said Forrester VP and principal analyst Charlie Dai.
That includes any adjustments that their Big Tech customers might make to their spending plans.
This past week, when Microsoft and Google forecast less AI spending than Wall Street analysts had projected, shares in several neocloud firms tumbled.
Much is also riding on Anthropic and OpenAI, which are both expected to start selling shares to the public in the months ahead.
If AI proves to be a bubble â and bursts â neocloud firms "are definitely going to face collateral damage," said Bradley Tusk of Tusk Ventures.
'Guppy-level death'
The future of the neoclouds also depend on their ability to keep borrowing, which gets more expensive as interest rates rise.
In a recent social media post, Elon Musk suggested this challenge could lead more than 200 neoclouds to "see guppy-level death and consolidation", with the smallest firms being the most vulnerable.
"Some will make it through, but not many," he added.
For now, analysts at Yorkville Ives said demand for computing power still exceeds supply, adding that neoclouds are filling an important gap that larger data centre companies cannot fill.
But to some, the neocloud sector's recent wobbles are concerning.
Microsoft recently cancelled a deal with a British neocloud outfit called Nscale amid power supply issues which could last through to 2030.
Australia's Firmus just shelved plans to start selling shares to the public.
These developments come amid a public backlash against data centres and questions about how much value AI can add to worker productivity.
"There's reason to worry," said Johnson.

articles.headline: Antonelli feeling 'tense' amid effort to seal F1 title

body: Kimi Antonelli: Mercedes driver admits to feeling 'tense' amid effort to seal F1 title at Mexico City Grand Prix

Kimi Antonelli needs top-nine finish to become world champion at Mexico City Grand Prix; he only qualified fifth and was off the pace compared to Mercedes team-mate George Russell; watch Sunday's race at 8pm (build-up from 6.30pm), live on Sky Sports F1
Sunday 1 November 2026 00:48, UK
Kimi Antonelli has admitted to feeling "more tense than usual" ahead of attempting to seal the Formula 1 world championship at Sunday's Mexico City Grand Prix.
The 20-year-old only needs to finish ninth in the race to become the sport's youngest world champion.
Antonelli qualified fifth on Saturday but will start from fourth on the grid due to a penalty for Max Verstappen.
Speaking after the session, the Italian revealed that he is not feeling his best as he continues to recover from an illness that caused him to miss his media duties on Thursday.
He told Sky Sports F1: "It has not been the easiest weekend to be fair.
"Definitely still not feeling 100 per cent. There is talk of what could happen [with the championship] and definitely I'm a bit more tense than usual.
"Definitely I don't feel as relaxed but I try to have a good sleep tonight and focus on tomorrow."
Despite his condition, Antonelli was still able to produce a decent final lap in qualifying as he finished within two tenths of pole-sitter Lewis Hamilton.
However, the fact that his team-mate George Russell was only marginally behind Hamilton in second perhaps reflected the Italian not being able to summon his best level.
Antonelli added: "I struggled to get a good feeling from the tyres in Q3. I just didn't have the most confidence. I was a bit tense, I am not going to lie.
"It was a poor lap, many mistakes here and there. Overall, still P4 and a lot to play for tomorrow."
'It's insane!' - Norris happy to pass No 1 onto Antonelli
Lando Norris says he is "more than happy" to pass the number one he has had on his McLaren this year to Antonelli when the Mercedes driver replaces him as world champion.
Antonelli has massively exceeded expectations during just his second season in F1 to comprehensively outperform Russell, who began the year as the clear title favourite.
"He's done an incredible job and done it in a pretty incredible way," Norris said ahead of the race weekend in Mexico.
"People are saying he hasn't had any tough competition this year. That proves the point that he's done such an incredible job.
"He's got a very, very talented team-mate that he's beaten through the whole season.
"I have nothing but respect for Kimi. He's a very nice guy. We get along very well and I'm more than happy to pass the No 1 over to him.
"He deserves it. He's done an incredible job, especially in his second year in Formula 1. Youngest world champion, it's pretty insane.
"I enjoy other people having that kind of success. It's nice to see."

articles.headline: This 'truly modular' keyboard can be built like a Lego set — meaning you can add as many keys as you like
keyFacts: MIT student Nathan Alspaugh developed Keybytes, an open-source keyboard project allowing users to create custom layouts using magnetically connected individual keys.
Alspaugh reported that each Keybit contains its own RISC-V microcontroller, while the central Keyword module uses an Arm Cortex-M4 microcontroller.
Alspaugh estimated that assembling a full-size version could cost approximately $900, though the project remains in an early stage.
body: - Keybytes lets users assemble custom keyboards from magnetically connected individual keys
- Every Keybit contains its own RISC-V microcontroller for individual key operation
- A full-size Keybytes configuration could cost approximately $900 to assemble
MIT student Nathan Alspaugh has developed Keybytes, an open source keyboard project that lets users create custom layouts by connecting individual keys to a central controller.
The design uses magnetic connections and dedicated microcontrollers to support flexible arrangements.
Keybytes consists of two main elements: the Keyword controller and individual Keybit modules, which connect magnetically to form a personalised keyboard.
Magnetic keys allow custom layouts
Each Keybit contains a RISC-V microcontroller, allowing individual keys to operate independently rather than relying entirely on one central processor.
Every Keybit measures 19.05 x 19.05mm, corresponding to a standard 1U keyboard unit.
Its four-sided pogo pin connections carry power and I2C communications, allowing modules to connect through different edges and accommodate varied arrangements.
The central Keyword module contains two stacked circuit boards, with an Arm Cortex M4 microcontroller.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The Keyword controller contains two stacked circuit boards, with its upper board housing an Arm Cortex-M4 microcontroller, a Bluetooth antenna and flash memory.
Its lower board provides USB-C connectivity, charging functions and a buck-boost converter for power management.
Each Keybit accommodates a Cherry MX mechanical switch, giving builders the option of selecting compatible switches for their preferred typing experience.
The magnetic connections allow keys to attach around the Keyword controller or alongside other modules, removing the fixed layout restrictions found in conventional keyboards.
Alspaugh has published the project files, design assets and construction details on GitHub under the permissive MIT licence.
This allows others to examine the design, build their own units and modify the hardware according to their requirements.
Building a full keyboard could cost $900
Despite its flexibility, Keybytes remains an early-stage project, with Alspaugh reporting that the basic system had only recently reached a working state.
Publicly available project documentation currently shows limited combinations of modules rather than a completed, full-size keyboard layout.
The developer estimated that assembling a full-size version using approximately 2 Keyword controllers and 110 Keybits would cost around $900.
That figure indicates how quickly expenses could accumulate when each additional key requires its own circuit board, microcontroller, and other electronic components.
Builders must also account for printed circuit board production, component purchases, soldering, and custom 3D-printed enclosures.
These requirements could make large layouts considerably more demanding than smaller configurations designed around a handful of shortcuts.
The current design also has limitations in its lighting options, since the Keyword includes a status indicator while individual Keybits lack dedicated illumination.

Future versions could add features such as customisable RGB lighting, rotary controls, fingerprint recognition modules or a compatible touchpad. These remain proposed additions rather than confirmed developments.

articles.headline: 5 expensive hobbies where owning a 3D printer actually saves you money
keyFacts: Engadget reported that owning a 3D printer can help hobbyists save money by producing affordable replacement parts and accessories on demand.
The article stated that 3D printers can reduce costs for hobbies like drone piloting, gardening, smart home automation, photography, and tabletop gaming.
Engadget advised considering equipment costs, running expenses, skill levels, and adequate ventilation space before investing in a 3D printer.
body: 5 expensive hobbies where owning a 3D printer actually saves you money
How owning a 3D printer can save you some big cash in your hobbies

NASA's 3D printers hosted on the International Space Station (ISS) print tools and replacement parts on demand. Here on Earth, 3D printers can sometimes make expensive components and accessories for a more affordable price than you can find in stores. However, does that make one worth buying?

3D printing (sometimes called additive manufacturing) uses computer-aided design (CAD) models sourced online or created by you to build three-dimensional objects. Entry-level printers like the Creality Ender-3 V3 SE cost from about $170, while more advanced systems reach $700 or more. The most common 3D printers use filament, which costs from around $20 per kilogram. If you make 50 $10 items from a kilo of filament on a $170 machine, you save money. Combine the cost of materials and hardware to calculate the cost to identify where you may save. You may not even need to own a printer as some libraries and maker spaces provide access, while online services will print for a price.

Most home printers use FDM (fused deposition modeling), where plastic filament, usually polylactic acid (PLA), is pushed through a heated nozzle to make something. More expensive 3D printers use resin (SLA/DLP, resin-based stereolithography and digital light processing, respectively) or polymer powder (SLS, selective laser sintering). The following ideas focus on how FDM printers save you money within a series of popular hobbies, but you'll want to upgrade to SLA printers where fine detail matters to you.
1. Replacement parts for drones

Drone or remote-controlled vehicle enthusiasts can save money printing spare parts for their machines — it's popular; some 3D modeling sites have entire sections for drone components. While you should not print flight-critical pieces (such as propellers) for your expensive drone until the material, design and strength have been validated, other parts (say, camera mounts, antenna guards and arm protectors) are fair game.

Anyone who has ever crash-landed their drone knows components require regular replacement, so if a part normally costs $10, a 3D printer that can churn it out for less will pay for itself over time. Not only that, but just like in the Space Station, the entire process may be cheaper and faster than ordering online.
2. 3D printing for gardeners and gearheads

If you work with vehicles or run a busy garden, your 3D printer is a real reservoir of solutions. Mechanic or horticulturist, you probably go through a host of replaceable components that may be cheaper to print than buy; this is particularly true when some are sold in larger quantities than anyone needs or are expensive because they're highly specialized.

From garden signage to plastic clips, planters to soil dibbers — even bird feeders — you'll find you can print many useful items. In the garage, print hard-to-find car interior pieces, broken knobs, tool organizers, wrenches and a multi-axis vise. The convenience of printing just the right tool for the job should save money, time and frustration in any garden or garage.
3. Print your way to a smarter home

The capacity to make the right tool for the job also makes 3D printers useful for home automation. You can print all the obvious things, including cable management systems, shelving for various hubs, wall mounts and small spare parts, but the tech also lets you indulge your taste for smart home projects.

For example, if you use near-field communication (NFC) stickers around your home to control smart devices, you can make them a lot less utilitarian and way more interesting by printing housings or button mechanisms for them. You can afford to be imaginative, like with a simple but useful Tap-for-Wi-Fi sign that uses NFC to provide guest access, but you may just want a desktop robot. If you want Apple-style home control, print the chassis for a Home Assistant touch screen at a fraction of the cost of Apple's $299 HomeView, or print a wall mount for almost any tablet.
4. 3D for photography and videography

Photography and video enthusiasts complain about the price some camera manufacturers charge for highly replaceable items like lens caps, cable clamps and battery holders. That changes with 3D printing; after all, why should a branded lens cap cost so much when you can print a universal lens cap for a few cents? Seek, and you will find 3D printing files for so many useful camera accessories.

Beyond replacement, print mechanical V-lock battery plates, custom microphone and lighting mounts, selfie handles or compact and portable tripods. What's really useful is that you can make or tweak CAD files to create single-use custom tools to grab specific shots.
5. Dungeons, dragons and railroads

Gamers, Dungeons & Dragons players, model railroad and scale modeling enthusiasts: 3D printing opens the doors to new fantasy experiences. Print new characters, monsters, buildings, trees, and terrain to make your next scenario sing, or boost your track layout with a railroad siding or long-lost logo. The vast trove of models at MyMiniFactory shows that a thriving trade in these things already exists. Tabletop gamers already print historically accurate uniformed troops for their next recreation — and likely need a resin printer for detail. Finally, and perhaps even more importantly, gamers may never lose their dice again.

While there are plenty of ways a 3D printer should make a difference, if you're considering investing in one for your hobby, do think about how often you'll use it, your skill when doing so, and the actual running costs before taking the leap. You also need space since 3D printers require plenty of ventilation, so don't use them in your lounge or bedroom. In most cases, the best place to begin is to work with someone else's printer to see if the tech is right for you.

The first week is where you begin your trade and set up your shop. First, pick a Specialization from the complete list of options available. Easiest one is Apprentice if you want things to begin smoothly.

Day 1

There will be five customers to attend, and you can call them using the green button near the recorder. At first, you’ll find your mentor who guides you about the basics. The customers who appear will be randomized, so the ones I encountered will be different from the ones you do.

Once again, I looked to purchase any food item they had, or discounted stuff they looked to sell for cheap. After the second day, you’ll be able to visit the Dumping Ground. Once you exhaust all attempts, pick the most valuable item and return.
Day 3

The final day of the first week has the highest number of clients to meet. Moreover, you’ll get to encounter someone named Wild, and you’ll learn about upgrades. Known as Wild’s Favours, you can pick from a wide variety of upgrades.
